title: Resolving coupled transport in space and time from molecular fluctuations in confined fluids
authors: Thê Hoang Ngoc Minh, Ian C. Bourg
abstract: Transport in fluids is generally reduced to continuum laws parametrized by bulk coefficients and effective interfacial parameters, such as viscosities, diffusivities, slip lengths, and interfacial resistances. This description becomes incomplete at the nanoscale, where spatial heterogeneity, molecular structure, and finite relaxation times are inseparable from the transport process. Here we formulate coupled transport in nanoconfined fluids as a space--time-resolved Onsager response matrix and extract it from equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations. Applied to a confined charged fluid, the framework resolves the nonlocal and transient pathways coupling particle, solute, heat, and charge transport. Momentum transport appears as a long-lived, nonlocal hydrodynamic mode, whereas charge transport relaxes rapidly through localized ionic friction. Off-diagonal responses reveal distinct projected dynamics, providing a microscopic basis for nonlocal, history-dependent transport laws.
summary: This work develops a sophisticated theoretical framework to calculate coupled transport phenomena in confined fluids by analyzing space-time correlations derived from molecular dynamics. By formulating the problem using an extended Onsager response matrix, the authors successfully distinguish between slow, nonlocal hydrodynamic modes and fast, localized ionic relaxation mechanisms. This provides crucial microscopic insights into how continuum theories break down at the nanoscale.
main_problem: The research aims to resolve coupled transport (particle, solute, heat, charge) in nanoconfined fluids by developing a framework that moves beyond continuum laws parameterized by bulk coefficients.
main_result: They demonstrate that hydrodynamic momentum transport is a long-lived nonlocal mode, while charge transport relaxes rapidly via localized ionic friction. The full space-time response kernel provides a microscopic basis for history-dependent transport laws.
method: The coupled transport is formulated as a space–time-resolved Onsager response matrix, extracted from equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations using generalized Green-Kubo relations.
model_or_system: The study uses a minimal model of a charged Lennard-Jones (LJ) fluid confined between two negatively-charged walls in a nanopore geometry. The analysis extends to coupling particle, solute, heat, and charge transport channels.
key_observables: Space–time response kernels ($R_{ab}(r, r', t)$), local–local responses ($G_{ab}$), off-diagonal electrokinetic couplings (Streaming Current, EOF), and the full 4x4 matrix of reduced response kernels.
important_parameters: Nanoscale confinement dimensions ($\sigma$), temperature ($k_B T$), and the time/space separation in correlation functions.
main_assumptions: The approach assumes that physics can be described by a generalized Onsager framework, relying on linear response theory applied to equilibrium current correlations. The analysis also involves choosing appropriate flux bases (e.g., excess flux basis).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the hierarchy of response functions from molecular dynamics simulations, showing snapshots of the charged fluid and detailed visualizations of the full 4x4 coupling matrix for different transport channels.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the generalized Onsager framework using equilibrium current correlations. It then analyzes specific couplings (hydrodynamic vs. charge) and explores how transforming to an 'excess flux basis' can suppress long-range hydrodynamic components, revealing underlying local relaxation mechanisms.
why_interesting: While focused on classical fluid dynamics, the rigorous application of linear response theory to derive non-equilibrium transport coefficients from microscopic fluctuations mirrors techniques used in quantum many-body physics for calculating correlation functions and transport properties in mesoscopic systems.
